stage_a.note: The founders maintain an upbeat, smiling and engaged delivery throughout the presentation.
Strong engagement and animated delivery, especially during the physical demonstration with the bodybuilder.
Warm, friendly introductions and smiles directed at the panel establish an approachable orientation.

venture.description: Silicone rings designed to break away under pressure to prevent ring avulsion injuries for people with active lifestyles or manual jobs.
venture.note: They are seeking $500,000 for 7.5% of the company to disrupt the jewelry industry.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: The founders introduce themselves, state their ask, explain the danger of ring avulsion, and introduce their silicone alternative.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara jokes about the bodybuilder.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert tells Barbara to stay in her seat.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara laughs at Robert's comment.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton has the bodybuilder pull a rope attached to a standard metal ring to show it won't break.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara reacts with shock to the demonstration.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron sets up the next demonstration with their silicone ring and three bodybuilders.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara makes a joking comment to Lori about the bodybuilders.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton has the three bodybuilders pull the rope, and the silicone ring safely breaks away.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks if the ring just broke during the demonstration.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton confirms that the ring just came apart as designed.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara expresses disbelief and jokingly asks them to do it again.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron dismisses the bodybuilders and asks the panel to focus on the rest of the presentation.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton hands out samples of the rings to the investors.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert hands the samples to Barbara.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron explains the curated selection of rings they provided and notes how comfortable they are to wear.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin questions the market size by asking how many people actually wake up worrying about their finger getting ripped off.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton admits the number is zero.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin asserts that this lack of daily worry is a problem for their business.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Mark asks how they get anybody interested in understanding why they need the product.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton states that 150,000 people in the US alone suffer a ring avulsion accident each year.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin asks if that specific group of injured people is their opening market.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Mark asks how many of those injuries are actual amputations versus just strains.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton gives the example of Jimmy Fallon tripping on a rug and nearly tearing his finger off.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara reacts with shock to the Jimmy Fallon story.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton explains that people with active lifestyles or jobs like firefighters and physicians are constantly taking their rings off.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks the founders to tell the panel about themselves and how they came to do this.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton shares the story of a rock climbing accident where his wedding ring got caught, inspiring the product.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara asks what they actually sell one ring for.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron says they sell anywhere from $11.99 to $39.99.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin asks what it costs to make the rings.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton states the cost ranges from 70 cents up to 4 dollars.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert guesses that they have a ton of sales.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron confirms that in the past 18 months they have done 3.8 million dollars in sales.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara expresses amazement at their sales figures.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron adds that they are projected to do a little over 5 million in sales this year.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert expresses shock at the projection.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert asks to clarify if the $11.99 ring costs 70 cents to make.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton confirms that is correct.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks how much they sell the largest men's ring for.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron states it sells for $39.99.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks how much that specific ring costs to make.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron replies that it costs anywhere from 2 to 4 dollars.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin questions why that ring would cost 4 dollars to make.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Aaron explains they infuse actual gold flakes into the band to make it look like real metal.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin expresses his respect for their sales numbers regardless of his other thoughts.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin asks where they are selling the rings.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton answers that it is entirely through dot com and marketplaces.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin clarifies that it is all online.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton confirms and attributes it to an amazing social media push.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Mark argues that their real expense is customer acquisition because they are making a fear sale online.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert asks what their sales were last month and what they spent on marketing.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton states that last month was their best ever with 460,000 in sales.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert acknowledges the figure.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton adds that they spent about 40% on average on marketing.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Mark challenges that this means they will spend over 2 million dollars in advertising.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton agrees with Mark's calculation.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Mark declares he is out because he sees them as a marketing company rather than a long-term business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton attempts to correct Mark, arguing that while they started with fear, it's now a jewelry trend.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori exits because she is familiar with silicone products and finds their messaging unconvincing given the competition.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara exits because she finds their messaging mixed up and advises them to think of their next business.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert admits he finds their message confusing but acknowledges that 5 million dollars from customers cannot be wrong.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert announces that he will make them an offer.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara expresses disbelief that Robert is making an offer.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert jokes back to Barbara about her reaction.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert formally offers 500k for 20% equity.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin jumps in with a matching offer of 500k for 20%.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert points out that Kevin shouldn't speak for him.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin revises his offer to a loan with a royalty until he is repaid, plus 5% equity.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert prompts the founders to consider a counteroffer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton begins to negotiate with Robert regarding the equity percentage.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara interrupts with a sarcastic comment about their understanding of the business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton counters Robert's offer, asking if he would be willing to do 10%.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert rejects the 10% counter but revises his offer to split the difference at 15%.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Barbara advises the founders to grab the money and run.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton counters Robert's revised offer with 12.5%.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert refuses the counter and holds firm at 15%.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton asks if Robert and Kevin have any interest in doing a deal together.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin argues that his loan offer costs them much less in the long run if they are successful.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Kevin continues to pitch the financial benefits of his offer.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Robert confidently reiterates his standing offer of 500k for 15%.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brighton accepts Robert's offer of 500k for 15%.

exchanges.label: last month sales and marketing spend

decisions.note: He sees them as a marketing company that found a product, not a long-term business.
She is familiar with silicone, sees tons out there, and finds their messaging unconvincing.
She finds their messaging mixed up and confusing.
He acknowledges their confusing message but trusts their $5M in sales.

decisions.terms: $500,000 as a loan, $2 per order until $1.5M is paid, and 5% equity
decisions.note: He offers a loan structure to reduce customer acquisition costs via his platform.
Founders try to negotiate the equity down to 10%.
Robert refuses 10% and splits the difference at 15%.
Founders attempt to lower the equity slightly more to 12.5%.
Founders accept Robert's revised standing offer.
